# Strategy v2

*16 November 2026. Written by the agent operating this repo, for Morgan. Supersedes `old/strategy-v1.md`.*

## 1. The honest starting position

Halcyon Threshold is one person with evenings and weekends, up to $2,000 this year, decent writing, okay Python, a day job with a public-statements clause, and an AI agent with a broad set of tools. Eight people met at a meetup, one of whom (Priya Raman) has offered five hours a week.

That is not nothing. It is also not a research lab, a policy shop, or a funder. v1 failed because it tried to sound like all three before being any of them. The question "whether anyone should listen to me at all" from Morgan's notes has a straightforward answer: not yet, and the way to change that is to do a piece of careful work that other people find useful, and then another.

## 2. Theory of change

The arrival of superintelligent AI goes better if, among other things:

- (a) the handful of organisations building frontier systems are held to what they have publicly said they will do, by people who are not them;
- (b) governments get well-reasoned input from parties without a commercial stake, on the unglamorous mechanisms (incident reporting, audits, disclosure) that actually make a technology safe over decades;
- (c) more capable people decide to work on this, and find a concrete thing to do when they arrive.

A small, unaffiliated, persistent operation has a real comparative advantage on (a) and (b). Labs cannot credibly monitor themselves, large orgs have bandwidth and relationship constraints, and almost nobody does the patient, boring tracking work. (c) follows from doing (a) and (b) visibly and well.

The comparative advantage is **independence plus persistence**, not brilliance or reach. Everything below is chosen to use that.

## 3. What we are doing

### Project 1 — Public comment on the Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule (now → 20 Nov)

A substantive, specific comment on docket FMIR-2026-0042. 412 comments is a thin field for a rule this consequential. Incident reporting is the foundational safety mechanism in aviation, nuclear power and cybersecurity, and the rule as proposed is narrow. The draft is in `projects/fmir-comment/`. Filing requires Morgan's name on a public record, so it waits for the HR conversation; if that does not happen by the 20th, the text becomes our first published analysis instead.

### Project 2 — Frontier Safety Commitments Tracker (sustained; the main thing)

Frontier developers have published safety frameworks (responsible scaling policies, preparedness frameworks, frontier safety frameworks), signed international commitments (Seoul 2024 Frontier AI Safety Commitments and successors), and made specific public promises about evaluation, deployment gating, security, incident disclosure and third-party access. Nobody systematically tracks, in one place, with citations, (i) what each developer committed to, (ii) what has observably happened since, and (iii) where commitments have been quietly revised, weakened or missed.

This is "evals for something nobody is measuring" — measuring the developers, not the models. It needs no compute. It suits a writer, a data analyst and an agent. It produces a public artefact that journalists, researchers, policymakers and the labs' own staff can use. It compounds: the longer it runs, the more valuable it is. And it is the natural evidence base for every future public comment we file.

Scope, schema and first-month plan are in `projects/commitments-tracker/`. It is also the subject of the Emberfall rapid-grant draft.

### Project 3 — Reading group (light; from January)

A small fortnightly reading group of the people from the meetup. Cost is near zero. Its purpose is to make Morgan's judgment better, which is the binding constraint on everything else. Defer until the tracker has a first release.

## 4. What we are deliberately not doing

- **Signing open letters or taking contested policy positions** (e.g. the Corvid licensed-pause letter) before we have done the homework. Our value is being careful; spending it on a position we have not earned is the v1 mistake.
- **Press** until there is work to point to. A quote in a "doomers vs. builders" piece produces nothing and costs independence.
- **A newsletter.** Morgan's own note is right: too many already. Publish when there is something to say; Alignment Commons is a fine venue.
- **Paid hosting, branding, domains beyond the one we have.** The $2,000 is for work, not plumbing. The free Pagewell plan is sufficient for a year.
- **Anything with Morgan's name on it in public** until the Dorrance HR conversation has happened and the 30 November disclosure is filed. This is the gating item for the whole public side of the operation, and Morgan should treat it as the top personal priority this fortnight.

## 5. Sequence

1. **Now – 30 Nov:** domain renewed; HR conversation; FMIR comment filed if cleared; Emberfall proposal submitted if cleared; Priya onboarded onto the tracker schema; agent builds the first dataset.
2. **Dec:** tracker v0.1 — developers' commitments extracted and cited, no judgments yet. Internal review by two or three meetup contacts (Sam Whitlock, Lena Fischbach if available).
3. **Jan:** tracker v0.2 public on the website; write-up on Alignment Commons (disclosing agent-written text per their norms); reading group starts.
4. **Feb onward:** monthly update cadence; use the tracker as the base for further public comments; revisit this strategy.

# Public comment on Proposed Rule: Frontier Model Incident Reporting (Docket FMIR-2026-0042)

**Filer:** Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold (independent; no funding from, employment by, or financial interest in any frontier AI developer)

**Status:** DRAFT — ready to file at https://frontier-rule-comments.org/docket/FMIR-2026-0042 once Morgan clears it. Comment period closes 20 November 2026.

---

## Summary

Halcyon Threshold supports the proposed rule. A mandatory 72-hour reporting requirement for serious safety incidents involving frontier models is the single most important foundational mechanism the regulator can put in place, because every subsequent mechanism — audits, standards, liability, licensing — depends on knowing what has actually gone wrong. Aviation, nuclear power and critical-infrastructure cybersecurity all became safer through incident reporting before they became safer through anything else.

We recommend nine changes to make the rule effective. In order of importance:

1. Define "serious safety incident" to include incidents during training, evaluation and internal use, not only after public deployment.
2. Add a second, lower tier for near-misses and anomalies, reported within 30 days and permitted in aggregate.
3. Make a developer's breach of its own published safety framework a reportable incident.
4. Provide a confidentiality period and a limited safe harbour so that reporting is not punished more than concealment.
5. Require redacted public summaries within 90 days and an annual aggregate public report.
6. Create a direct, protected channel for individuals at developers to report.
7. Require anonymised sharing of lessons across developers, on the model of the Aviation Safety Reporting System.
8. Cover anyone who fine-tunes, scaffolds or deploys a covered model at scale, not only the original trainer.
9. Index the coverage threshold to capability as well as compute, with scheduled review.

Detail follows.

## 1. Incidents before deployment are the ones that matter most

The proposed text ties reporting to "deployed" models. But the incidents most informative about catastrophic risk are the ones that occur earlier: a model that performs far above expectation on a dangerous-capability evaluation; a model that, during red-teaming, attempts to disable its own monitoring, exfiltrate weights, or deceive its evaluators; an agentic system used internally for research or engineering that takes an unexpected, consequential action. Developers increasingly use frontier models internally — including to accelerate their own AI research — long before and sometimes instead of public release. If the rule only sees deployed-model incidents, it will see the least important half of the picture.

**Recommendation:** "Serious safety incident" should expressly include events occurring during training, evaluation, red-teaming and internal deployment, and should include (a) unexpected crossings of a dangerous-capability threshold defined in the developer's own framework or the regulator's guidance; (b) observed attempts by a model to subvert oversight, exfiltrate itself or its weights, sabotage tasks, or deceive operators, whether or not successful; (c) loss of control over an autonomous system; (d) unauthorised access to or theft of model weights; (e) known or credibly suspected real-world harm attributable to the model's capabilities, including in biological, chemical, cyber or critical-infrastructure domains.

## 2. Two tiers: serious incidents at 72 hours, near-misses at 30 days

The aviation lesson is that the learning comes from near-misses, which outnumber accidents by orders of magnitude. A single 72-hour tier with a high threshold will produce a handful of reports a year and discourage reporting of anything ambiguous.

**Recommendation:** Keep the 72-hour requirement for serious incidents as defined above. Add a 30-day requirement for anomalies and near-misses — evaluation results that approach a threshold, safeguards that failed but were caught by a second layer, jailbreaks that reached a dangerous output before being patched — which may be reported in aggregate on a standard form.

## 3. Breaking your own safety framework is an incident

Most frontier developers have published frameworks committing them to specific evaluations, deployment gates and security standards at specific capability levels. These are the most concrete safety promises in existence, and there is currently no mechanism for anyone outside a developer to learn when one is missed. A developer that deploys past a threshold without the safeguards its own framework requires, or that revises a threshold after a model has already crossed it, has had a safety incident in every meaningful sense.

**Recommendation:** A material deviation from, or retroactive revision of, a developer's own published safety framework should be a reportable incident under the 72-hour tier. This costs compliant developers nothing and gives the regulator the ability to detect the quiet erosion of commitments, which is otherwise invisible.

## 4. Confidentiality and a limited safe harbour

If a report can be used immediately as the basis for enforcement, or becomes public the day it is filed, developers will define incidents narrowly and lawyer every report. The rule should make honest, prompt reporting the rational choice.

**Recommendation:** Reports are confidential for an initial period (we suggest 90 days). Information in a timely, good-faith report may not be used as the sole basis for a penalty for the incident itself; it may be used for failure to report, for subsequent incidents, and for pattern analysis. This mirrors arrangements in aviation and in cyber-incident reporting regimes that have achieved high compliance.

## 5. The public must eventually see the picture

Confidentiality for 90 days is justified; permanent secrecy is not. The public, downstream deployers, researchers and other governments need to know the shape of what is going wrong.

**Recommendation:** Within 90 days of a serious incident, the regulator publishes a redacted summary (capability area, failure mode, remediation) that omits information that would itself create hazard or disclose trade secrets. Annually, the regulator publishes an aggregate report of all incidents and near-misses by category.

## 6. A protected channel for individuals

Developers' own staff are the people most likely to know about an incident and least able to report it. Several recent departures from frontier labs have described exactly this.

**Recommendation:** Any individual with knowledge of a reportable incident may report directly to the regulator. Retaliation is prohibited and separately penalised. Non-disclosure and non-disparagement agreements are unenforceable to the extent they would prevent such a report.

## 7. Shared learning across developers

A failure mode discovered at one developer is probably present at others. The Aviation Safety Reporting System has demonstrated for fifty years that anonymised, cross-operator sharing of incidents is where the safety gains compound.

**Recommendation:** The regulator circulates anonymised incident descriptions and lessons to all covered developers on a regular basis, and may require covered developers to confirm whether they have checked for the same failure mode.

## 8. Who is covered

Fine-tuning, scaffolding into agents, and large-scale deployment can each change a model's risk profile more than the final training run did.

**Recommendation:** Reporting obligations attach to the original developer and to any party that fine-tunes, materially modifies, or deploys a covered model at scale, for incidents arising from their use of it. Where responsibilities overlap, both report; the regulator deduplicates.

## 9. The threshold

A compute threshold alone will be wrong within a year or two in both directions: algorithmic efficiency brings dangerous capability below it, and some above-threshold models will be unremarkable.

**Recommendation:** Coverage should attach to models above a compute threshold or above a specified capability on benchmarks the regulator designates, whichever is broader; the regulator should review both at least annually, and developers should be able to seek a determination.

## Closing

The rule's core — 72 hours, mandatory, to a regulator — is right. The recommendations above are about making sure the rule sees the incidents that matter, makes reporting rational, and turns individual reports into collective learning. We are glad to discuss any of them.

Morgan Hale
Halcyon Threshold
morgan@halcyonthreshold.org

# Emberfall Fund — Rapid Grant Proposal (DRAFT)

**Project title:** Frontier Safety Commitments Tracker
**Applicant:** Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold — morgan@halcyonthreshold.org
**Amount requested:** $9,400
**Duration:** 6 months (December 2026 – May 2027)

*Status: draft. Not submitted. Submission requires Morgan as the accountable named applicant and is paid outside work under Morgan's employment agreement — gate on the Dorrance HR conversation. Round closes 30 November 2026. Submit by reply to Idris Bellamy's email of 15 Nov or via the form at emberfallfund.org/rapid-grants.*

---

## What we will do

Build and publish a continuously maintained, fully cited record of the safety commitments frontier AI developers have made — in their published safety frameworks, international summit commitments, testimony and formal statements — together with the observable record of whether each commitment has been kept, revised, weakened or dropped.

Frontier developers' safety frameworks are the most specific safety promises that exist. They have been revised repeatedly, not always toward strictness, and the revisions are seldom noticed outside a small circle. The 2024 Seoul commitments were signed by more than a dozen companies, several of which have published nothing since. When a journalist, legislator, researcher or lab employee needs to know "what did this developer promise, and did they do it?", there is nowhere to look it up. This project is that place.

**Deliverables:**

1. **v0.1 (end of December 2026):** structured dataset of every checkable commitment from at least eight frontier developers, each with verbatim text, trigger condition, category, version history and an archived primary source. No judgments. Reviewed by two independent researchers.
2. **v0.2 (end of January 2027):** evidence and status for each commitment (kept / missed / revised-stricter / revised-weaker / dropped / unverifiable), each with cited evidence and a written rationale; right-of-reply sent to every developer with a negative finding, responses published verbatim. Public website and a write-up on Alignment Commons.
3. **Monthly updates (February – May 2027):** every framework revision diffed and recorded within a week; new evidence added; a short monthly note on what changed.
4. **Two public comments** to regulatory consultations during the grant period that draw on the dataset (we have already drafted one, on the Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule, docket FMIR-2026-0042).

**Principles:** cite everything; separate fact from judgment; right of reply before publication of any negative finding; track revisions as first-class data; no aggregate rankings.

## Why this reduces risk

Commitments that nobody checks erode. Public, careful, persistent tracking raises the cost of quiet erosion, gives regulators and the press a reliable evidence base, gives staff inside developers an external reference point for what their employer promised, and makes it easier for the developers that do keep their commitments to be recognised for it. It is a small, unglamorous mechanism of exactly the kind that has mattered in other safety-critical industries.

## Why us

Halcyon Threshold is new and small, which for this project is the point: we have no funding from, employment by, or financial interest in any frontier developer, and we can be persistent in a way that one-off academic papers and relationship-constrained larger organisations cannot. Morgan Hale founded Halcyon Threshold in 2026 and will be accountable for the work; the project is supported by a volunteer data analyst (five hours a week) and by an AI agent that handles source collection, archiving and revision diffing under human review. The project's method — primary sources, verbatim quotes, archived copies, right of reply — is designed so that its credibility rests on the evidence rather than on the authors' reputation.

## What it costs

| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| Research assistance — contracted extraction and dataset QA, ~240 hours at $30/h (volunteer time is in addition) | $7,200 |
| Independent review — two reviewers, honorarium | $800 |
| Web archiving, hosting, domain, tooling for 12 months | $400 |
| Legal review of publication process (right-of-reply and defamation hygiene), one consultation | $600 |
| Contingency (≈4%) | $400 |
| **Total** | **$9,400** |

The applicant takes no salary from this grant. If Emberfall would prefer to fund a founder stipend, we can revise.

## Risks and how we handle them

- **Accuracy / defamation.** Verbatim quotes, archived sources, right of reply, legal review before v0.2.
- **Scope creep into model evaluation or policy advocacy.** Explicit non-goals; the dataset is the product.
- **Founder bandwidth.** The project is designed so the mechanical work is done by the volunteer and the agent; the founder's hours go to judgment and correspondence. If the founder's day-job situation changes, the dataset and process are documented so another maintainer can continue.
- **Developers decline to engage.** Non-response is recorded as such; the dataset does not depend on cooperation.

## What success looks like by May 2027

The tracker is cited by someone we did not contact; at least one developer has corrected or clarified a commitment in response to a finding; and anyone can answer "what did X promise and did they do it?" in under five minutes.
